blocks.text: Real data almost never arrives with column names you actually want to type over and over. You get 'Order Total', 'Cust Name  ', or a CSV with no header row at all. Fixing this up front saves you from fighting awkward column names for the rest of your analysis, and pandas makes it quick.

blocks.caption: The most direct way to fix a handful of specific column names.

blocks.text: rename() takes a dict mapping old column names to new ones. Only the columns you mention get renamed, everything else stays as is.

blocks.caption: Like most pandas methods, this does not touch the original DataFrame unless you tell it to.

blocks.title: rename does not mutate by default
blocks.content: rename() returns a new DataFrame, following the general pandas convention of preferring non mutating operations. It does accept inplace=True, but reassigning the result, df = df.rename(...), is the more common and generally recommended style.

blocks.caption: The reassignment style keeps your code easier to trace, which is why it is the more common convention.

blocks.text: When you want to replace every single column name, reassigning df.columns directly to a new list is simpler than building a rename dict. This comes up often right after reading a CSV that had no header row, where pandas assigns numeric column names by default.

blocks.caption: Fast when you are renaming everything, not just a couple of columns.

blocks.title: The new list must match the existing column count exactly
blocks.content: If your new list has a different length than the number of existing columns, pandas raises a ValueError rather than guessing what you meant.

blocks.caption: Always double check df.shape[1] matches the length of your new list first.

blocks.text: 3. Cleaning Up Messy Column Names Programmatically
A very common real world pattern is cleaning up every column name in one pass using the same .str accessor methods you would use on any text column, applied directly to df.columns.

blocks.alt: Cleaning Up Messy Column Names Programmatically
blocks.caption: One line fixes case, whitespace, and spacing across every column at once.

blocks.alt: Cleaning Up Messy Column Names Programmatically
blocks.caption: This is what most real world column cleanup actually looks like.

blocks.text: rename_axis() renames the index itself, not the columns. It comes up less often, but it is worth knowing it exists, especially once your index carries real meaning, like a customer_id you set as the index.

blocks.caption: Useful once your index is a real identifier, not just a default range.

blocks.text: 5. Worked Example: Cleaning a CSV's Column Names

Say you read a CSV and end up with columns like ' Order  Total', 'CustName', and 'Region '. A single cleanup pass handles the general mess, then a manual rename fixes up one column that still needs a clearer name.

code.content:
df.columns = df.columns.str.lower().str.strip().str.replace(" ", "_")
# columns are now: order__total, custname, region

df = df.rename(columns={"custname": "customer_name"})

blocks.alt: Worked Example: Cleaning a CSV's Column Names
blocks.caption: A cleanup pass handles the bulk of the mess, a targeted rename finishes the job.

blocks.alt: Worked Example: Cleaning a CSV's Column Names
blocks.caption: Both techniques together, which is exactly how you would do this in a real script.

items: rename(columns={...}) renames specific columns and returns a new DataFrame by default.
Reassigning df.columns replaces every column name at once, but the new list length must match exactly.
A chained str.lower/strip/replace pass is the standard way to programmatically clean up messy column names.
rename_axis() renames the index itself, separate from the column names.
Combine a programmatic cleanup pass with a targeted manual rename for the best of both.
